{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"Ownership means control that survives the checkout screen. If a maker can switch off a feature after you have paid, you bought an object with a remote hand still wrapped around its throat. The device sits on your desk, but its capabilities don't belong entirely to you. That is the governing problem.

You can call this a software update, a safety measure, or a service decision. The label doesn't settle the question. If you own a car, a camera, or a phone, you expect the thing you bought to keep doing the things you bought it to do. You may accept repairs, recalls, or an honest replacement program. You won't accept a seller reaching through time and removing part of the bargain. A seller–buyer bargain that leaves the seller with a kill switch is a peculiar sale indeed.

Here's the trick: the feature is presented as a property of the device, then treated as a permission from the maker. You paid for the camera, but the maker decides whether the camera may see. You paid for storage, but the maker decides how much of it you may use. You paid for a tool, but the maker keeps the key. Ownership under those terms means possession without authority, like being handed a house whose rooms can be locked from another city.

I think the sharpest test is simple. Ask whether your control continues when the maker changes its mind. If it doesn't, your purchase contains a dependency that the checkout page concealed. I don't mean every change is abusive. A vulnerability may require a shutdown; a legal order may constrain a service; a broken component may need replacement. But those cases need clear limits, notice, and a path for you to keep using what you paid for. They can't turn a general promise of ownership into a temporary invitation (even when the reason sounds respectable).

People have accepted this arrangement because software makes the intrusion feel weightless. A button disappears. A menu greys out. A server rejects a request. Nothing dramatic happens in the room, so the loss feels imaginary. Yet the result is physical. The appliance cooks fewer meals. Your vehicle loses a function. Your phone becomes a shell around a decision made elsewhere. The law should call that what it is: a reduction in the thing you possess.

The usual defense is that connected products need ongoing management. Fair enough. Owners need security patches, bug fixes, and safeguards against genuine harm. But ongoing support is different from ongoing permission. A mechanic who repairs your bicycle doesn't reserve the right to remove its brakes next year. A landlord who changes a lightbulb doesn't acquire the right to shrink your kitchen. The network may be involved in operating a device; it doesn't follow that the network owns the device's future (the distinction matters most when the service disappears).

I have little patience for the polished language that turns this distinction into bullshit. “Experience management” can describe a useful improvement, or it can hide a product being quietly withdrawn. “Dynamic capability control” can sound technical, while its practical meaning is blunt: your seller can take something back. Rules should force makers to disclose such powers before purchase, identify which functions depend on a server–dependent feature, and preserve local operation where safety allows it.

Our response should also be practical. You should ask, before buying, which features work offline, what happens when an account closes, and whether an update can remove a function. Keep manuals, receipts, and the original feature list. Support repair, interoperability, and tools that let owners inspect and maintain their devices. I want that last point stated plainly because it changes the balance: when owners can repair and operate a device without permission, they hold something closer to ownership (where safety allows).

The principle is older than any app store. A purchase should transfer meaningful control, rather than merely place a branded object in your hands. We can tolerate limits that are specific, disclosed, and tied to real safety. We shouldn't tolerate a contract that calls you an owner while reserving the power to revoke the object’s useful parts. I return to the image of the remote hand because it makes the politics visible. If a device can be disabled from afar, ownership is conditional. Ownership means control that survives the checkout screen. If a maker can switch off a feature after you have paid, you bought an object with a remote hand still wrapped around its throat. The device sits on your desk, but its capabilities don't belong entirely to you. That is the governing problem.

You can call this a software update, a safety measure, or a service decision. The label doesn't settle the question. If you own a car, a camera, or a phone, you expect the thing you bought to keep doing the things you bought it to do. You may accept repairs, recalls, or an honest replacement program. You won't accept a seller reaching through time and removing part of the bargain. A seller–buyer bargain that leaves the seller with a kill switch is a peculiar sale indeed.

Here's the trick: the feature is presented as a property of the device, then treated as a permission from the maker. You paid for the camera, but the maker decides whether the camera may see. You paid for storage, but the maker decides how much of it you may use. You paid for a tool, but the maker keeps the key. Ownership under those terms means possession without authority, like being handed a house whose rooms can be locked from another city.

I think the sharpest test is simple. Ask whether your control continues when the maker changes its mind. If it doesn't, your purchase contains a dependency that the checkout page concealed. I don't mean every change is abusive. A vulnerability may require a shutdown; a legal order may constrain a service; a broken component may need replacement. But those cases need clear limits, notice, and a path for you to keep using what you paid for. They can't turn a general promise of ownership into a temporary invitation (even when the reason sounds respectable).

People have accepted this arrangement because software makes the intrusion feel weightless. A button disappears. A menu greys out. A server rejects a request. Nothing dramatic happens in the room, so the loss feels imaginary. Yet the result is physical. The appliance cooks fewer meals. Your vehicle loses a function. Your phone becomes a shell around a decision made elsewhere. The law should call that what it is: a reduction in the thing you possess.

The usual defense is that connected products need ongoing management. Fair enough. Owners need security patches, bug fixes, and safeguards against genuine harm. But ongoing support is different from ongoing permission. A mechanic who repairs your bicycle doesn't reserve the right to remove its brakes next year. A landlord who changes a lightbulb doesn't acquire the right to shrink your kitchen. The network may be involved in operating a device; it doesn't follow that the network owns the device's future (the distinction matters most when the service disappears).

I have little patience for the polished language that turns this distinction into bullshit. “Experience management” can describe a useful improvement, or it can hide a product being quietly withdrawn. “Dynamic capability control” can sound technical, while its practical meaning is blunt: your seller can take something back. Rules should force makers to disclose such powers before purchase, identify which functions depend on a server–dependent feature, and preserve local operation where safety allows it.

Our response should also be practical. You should ask, before buying, which features work offline, what happens when an account closes, and whether an update can remove a function. Keep manuals, receipts, and the original feature list. Support repair, interoperability, and tools that let owners inspect and maintain their devices. I want that last point stated plainly because it changes the balance: when owners can repair and operate a device without permission, they hold something closer to ownership (where safety allows).

The principle is older than any app store. A purchase should transfer meaningful control, rather than merely place a branded object in your hands. We can tolerate limits that are specific, disclosed, and tied to real safety. We shouldn't tolerate a contract that calls you an owner while reserving the power to revoke the object’s useful parts. I return to the image of the remote hand because it makes the politics visible. If a device can be disabled from afar, ownership is conditional. Our demand should be equally visible: sell us devices whose functions remain ours. That is repair–ownership policy in plain language.
